Our highly responsive team will be in touch with you shortly. Frequently Asked Questions Common questions about window installation for Utah homes. Should I replace all my windows at once? Not necessarily. Some homeowners replace all of their windows at the same time, while others replace the oldest or least efficient windows first. JDI Windows can help you determine which windows should be prioritized based on their condition, your goals, and your budget. What are the best replacement windows for Utah homes? Energy-efficient windows that can handle Utah’s hot summers, freezing winters, strong sunlight, and temperature swings are generally a good choice. JDI Windows installs vinyl replacement windows designed for durability, insulation, and year-round performance in Utah’s climate. Are vinyl windows good for Utah's climate? Yes. Quality vinyl windows are well suited for Utah because they provide good insulation, require little maintenance, and resist moisture and weathering. Energy-efficient glass options can provide additional protection against Utah’s seasonal temperature changes. Will replacing my windows help lower my energy bills? Energy-efficient replacement windows can help reduce heat transfer and air leakage, which can make it easier to heat and cool your home. Actual savings vary based on your existing windows, insulation, HVAC system, home, and the replacement windows selected. Can windows be replaced during the winter in Utah? Yes. Window replacement can be completed during colder months. Professional installers work efficiently to minimize the amount of time each opening is exposed to outdoor temperatures. Can you replace a window without replacing the entire frame? In some situations, a replacement window can use the existing opening and portions of the existing frame. If there is significant deterioration, water damage, or structural damage, additional work may be necessary. JDI Windows can inspect the existing window and recommend the appropriate replacement approach. How long do replacement windows last? The lifespan of replacement windows depends on the window materials, installation quality, weather exposure, and maintenance. High-quality vinyl windows that are properly installed can provide decades of service. Is replacing old windows worth it? Replacing old or inefficient windows can improve comfort, reduce drafts, improve curb appeal, and increase energy efficiency. Whether replacement makes sense depends on the condition of your current windows and your plans for the home. What should I look for in a window replacement company? Look for an experienced, licensed and insured window company that provides clear estimates, quality products, professional installation, warranty information, and strong local customer reviews. Choosing the right installer is important because even a quality window may not perform properly if it is installed incorrectly. What is the difference between replacement windows and new-construction windows? Replacement windows are designed to fit into an existing window opening, while new-construction windows are typically installed when a home is being built or when the existing window opening and surrounding materials are being substantially changed. The right option depends on the condition of your existing frames, the window opening, and the scope of the project. JDI Windows can evaluate your current windows and recommend the appropriate installation method. What happens if you find water damage when replacing a window? If water damage or deterioration is discovered around a window during replacement, it should be evaluated before the new window is fully installed. The amount of additional work needed depends on the extent and location of the damage. Properly addressing problems around the opening helps ensure the replacement window can be installed and sealed correctly. Do replacement windows need to be custom measured for my home? Yes. Accurate measurements are important because window openings can vary, even when the windows appear to be the same size. Measuring each opening helps ensure the replacement windows fit properly, operate correctly, and can be effectively sealed against outside air and moisture. This guide explains why fall is the right season for residential window replacement, what it actually costs to replace your windows, and what to watch out for during the home window replacement process. Contact JDI Windows Why fall works better than spring Sealants and caulk need moderate temperatures to cure properly. If it’s too hot, they set too fast and don’t bond correctly. If it’s too cold, they barely set at all. Fall usually gives installers that in-between window of decent weather, and that’s exactly when a residential window replacement holds up best over time. There’s also less competition for a spot on the schedule. Spring is when snowmelt reveals every problem a house had all winter, and every window company’s phone rings at once. Fall doesn’t have that rush. Crews have more room, which means you get your pick of dates instead of whatever’s left over. And the payoff starts immediately. Windows installed in October are already doing their job by the first hard freeze. Windows installed in April spend a whole heating season leaking before they ever help you. How the process actually goes Getting your windows replaced isn’t complicated, but there’s a sequence worth knowing. A contractor walks through your house. They look at frame condition and glass type and examine how your current windows are performing. Accurate measurements get taken. Guessing here is how homeowners end up with windows that don’t fit right. You pick your product. Frame material, glass package, and U-factor rating are all determined by your house and budget. Rebate eligibility gets checked. This should happen before you buy, not after, since rebate programs have specific product requirements. Installation gets scheduled. For fall timing, earlier is better, as it gives you more runway before winter weather sets in. Most homeowners can go from first phone call to finished installation in a matter of weeks, not months, especially in the fall when calendars aren’t backed up. What this looks like in real homes A home up at elevation with older aluminum-frame, single-pane windows behaves differently from a newer build with double-pane vinyl that recently lost its seal. The aluminum-frame house usually loses heat through the frame itself as much as through the glass since aluminum conducts cold straight through. The newer home with a failed seal is dealing with a narrower problem: fog between the panes , but the frame and the rest of the envelope are still doing their job. Here in Utah County, older homes with original single-pane windows tend to see the most noticeable difference after a home window replacement, simply because they had the most ground to make up. Newer homes with one or two failed units see a smaller jump in comfort, but still eliminate fogging and the cold spot by the window for good. Why upgrading your windows matters While upgrading your windows certainly has visual appeal, the benefits go far beyond that, saving you money and improving your resale value if you decide to sell. Here’s a rundown: Cuts the amount of energy your heating and cooling system has to work for Gets rid of drafts and cold spots near windows in winter Removes the fogged, cloudy look that comes with a failed seal Adds to your home’s resale value when it’s time to sell Reduces the risk of water damage that comes with long-term seal failure Makes a visible difference in curb appeal, especially on older homes There’s also a comfort difference most homeowners don’t expect until it’s gone. New windows substantially cut down on outside noise. A properly sealed double-pane unit cuts outside noise from traffic and wind. It also reduces other street sounds that come through single-pane glass. In homes along busier stretches of the Wasatch Front, that alone changes how a room feels. It’s not something a rebate program measures, but it’s often the first thing people notice after installation. Replacing single-pane windows with ENERGY STAR-certified products can reduce heating and cooling costs by up to 13% nationwide, according to ENERGY STAR’s own figures . Vinyl window replacement recoups roughly 67–72% of project cost at resale, according to the 2025 Remodeling Cost vs. Value Report from Zonda . What to look for before you sign anything U-factor rating: Utility rebate programs in Utah generally require a score of 0.22 or lower, so ask for this number rather than an “efficient” label. ENERGY STAR certification: This is the baseline most rebate programs check for. Frame material fit for your house. Vinyl, fiberglass, and wood all perform differently in temperature swings. A written, line-item quote. You should be able to see exactly what you’re paying for. Installer credentials. Ask who’s actually doing the install. Warranty terms in writing. Get the specifics on what’s covered and for how long. FAQ Q: How long does residential window replacement usually take? Most single-family homes are done in one to three days for a full-house project, depending on the number of windows and frame type. Q: Is there still a tax credit for window replacement in 2026? No. The federal credit expired at the end of 2025. Utility rebates through Rocky Mountain Power and Enbridge Gas are still active and worth checking. Q: Do I need to replace all my windows at once? No. Plenty of homeowners replace their windows in phases, starting with the worst-performing rooms first. Q: What U-factor should I be looking for? Utah utility rebate programs generally require a rating of 0.22 or lower for ENERGY STAR-certified windows. Ready to get this done? Contact JDI Windows You know your windows better than anyone. July 15, 2026 jdiwindows Most people don’t think about their windows until one starts letting in cold air, or they’ve got one over the sink they can barely reach to open. Then the question arises: should you stick with a standard window or step up to a casement window ? This blog walks through both, covering how each seals, how each opens, what each runs, and where each belongs. By the end, you’ll know which fits your place. Table of Contents Toggle The difference between casement vs. standard windows How casement vs. standard windows compare Where each one belongs Where people go wrong What the energy side tells us What to ask before you buy Frequently asked questions Why does it matter more in Utah? Call JDI Windows today The difference between casement vs. standard windows A casement hangs on a side hinge and swings out like a door. You open it with a crank instead of sliding a sash. We build custom casement windows to the exact size of your window opening, which is why we use them for odd dimensions, older framing, or when someone wants a single pane of glass for the view instead of a bar across the middle. Standard windows are what most homes already have. Double-hung windows have two sashes that slide up and down, while sliders move side to side. Both come in stock sizes, so they’re cheaper and quicker to get. The difference comes down to how each one closes. A casement cranks tight against weatherstripping on all four sides. A standard window seal where one sash slides past another, and that joint lets more air through. It lets through more as the window ages and the hardware loosens. How casement vs. standard windows compare Here’s the side-by-side. Casements seal better. The four-sided seal keeps drafts out better than a sliding sash does. In winter, when the wind comes down the canyons, you feel that through the glass. Casements move more air. They open the whole pane, and you can angle them to catch a breeze. A standard window only opens half its opening at a time, so you get about half the airflow. At the same time, standard windows are simpler to run. You push them by hand. There’s less hardware, so there’s less to adjust or replace down the road. A casement’s crank is easy over a sink or counter, but it’s one more moving part. Standard windows are easier to clean up high. Double-hung windows tilt in, so you clean both sides from inside, which is handy on a second story. A casement you crank open and reach around the outside, which is more of a stretch. Finally, standard windows cost less. The different parts and custom sizing add to the cost of a casement. How much depends on frame material, glass, and size, so ask for the quote broken down line by line. Where each one belongs We recommend using a casement window in the following situations: When you want the tightest seal and the most air When the opening is an odd size that a stock window won’t fill Over a kitchen sink, where a crank is easier than a shove When you want one clean pane on a view Use a standard window with these considerations: When the budget is the main thing When the window opens over a walkway or patio Where an outward swing would be in the way When the room runs on a window-unit AC A traditional look on an older home is another good reason to stick with the standard. A casement won’t take a window AC. Since it swings out, there’s no flat surface to set the unit on. Where people go wrong We see a few issues when customers decide which window works best for them: People put a casement where it swings out over a walkway or patio . Then it’s in the way every time someone passes. People think custom means a long wait. It doesn’t. The opening gets measured, the window gets built to it, and a good shop turns it around without much extra time. People skip the frame material conversation. Vinyl, fiberglass, and wood each handle our freeze-thaw swings differently, and that choice matters more than crank versus slide. People buy on sticker price alone. The cheapest standard window loses more in air leakage over ten winters than it saved the day it went in. What the energy side tells us The U.S. Department of Energy points to windows as a major pathway for heat moving in and out of a house, and to air leakage around and through them as a major contributor to that loss. Cut the leakage, and you cut the bill. That’s where a casement’s seal has the edge over a sliding standard window. One thing worth saying plainly: the seal only works if the install is right. A window set square, flashed, and sealed does its job. A rushed install gives the advantage back, no matter which style you bought. The install moves your energy use more than the style does. What to ask before you buy Casement window installation comes down to the details, so ask whoever’s quoting you: Are you measuring each opening, or fitting a stock size into it? How’s the unit getting flashed and sealed against water? What frame material do you use up here, and why that one? What’s the warranty on the crank hardware, not only the glass? Frequently asked questions Q: Do custom casement windows cost more than standard windows? Usually, yes. The crank, the hinges, and the custom sizing add up. How much depends on size, frame, and glass. Ask for a written, itemized estimate. Q: Can I put a window AC unit in a casement window? No. It swings outward, so there’s no flat opening for the unit. Q: Is casement window installation harder than a standard window? It takes more care. The unit has to sit square and sealed so the crank runs smoothly and the seal actually seals. It’s routine work for us, but it’s not the place to hand the job to the lowest bidder. Q: Which lasts longer, casement or standard? Both go decades when they’re put in the right way. A casement has moving hardware that’ll want adjusting eventually. A standard window has fewer parts. Frame material and install quality decide this more than the style does. Why does it matter more in Utah? Utah weather puts a sharper point on the sealing question than milder places deal with. Along the Wasatch Front, winter wind and hard freezes drive air through any gap they find, so a casement’s tight seal earns its keep on the coldest nights. In homes at elevation, the freeze-thaw cycle wears down frames and seals season after season. That’s why the frame material and a clean install matter as much as which style you pick.
